extracted.intended_audience: educated Christian readers, clergy, natural philosophers, and skeptics interested in the philosophical/theological defense of bodily resurrection
extracted.subtask_description: A philosophical-theological method for showing the possibility (and answering objections) of the Christian doctrine of bodily resurrection by appeal to natural observations, experiments, analogies, Scripture, and reasoned replies to common objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounding the argument in observed experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Use common experiments and observable natural phenomena (e.g., turn up the earth, rain/dew impregnating soil, preservation by cold or spirits, chemical reactions) to show how particles move, are preserved, or re-united.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author repeatedly appeals to everyday and chemical experiments (exposure of earth to air, rain carrying particles, preservation in cold or spirits of wine, saltpetre experiments) as sufficient to show that the dispersal and re-collection of material particles is not impossible; present concrete experimental instances to support claims about natural possibility rather than relying purely on abstract speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of analogies to familiar natural processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ analogies (seed/grain, optical image formed by rays of light, watch/skeleton reassembly, plant propagation diversity) to make the resurrection intelligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies should be concrete and drawn from widely observed phenomena: e.g., 'a grain of corn' as comparison for change in body, light rays forming an exact image despite mixing, a watchmaker reassembling a watch from parts, and the many ways plants reproduce—use these to show reassembly is not metaphysically impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic enumeration and rebuttal of objections
rubrics_metrics.description: List foreseeable objections (particles scattered or changed, cannibalism, consumption of bodies, wasting of bodies, identity concerns) and answer them one by one using natural, physiological, chemical, and theological points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the defense by naming each objector's difficulty and replying with empirical analogues or theoretical points; the text models responding to many named objections (e.g., particles turned into other bodies; parts dispersed over the earth; cannibalism) rather than ignoring them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to chemical/alchemical continuity of particles
rubrics_metrics.description: Show by chemical examples that 'spirits' or particles can undergo many unions and separations yet retain identity or be recoverable (e.g., nitrous spirit/saltpetre experiments, precipitation, crystallization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use descriptions of chemical operations (dissolution, precipitation, crystallization, filtration, distillation) as analogues indicating that metamorphoses do not rule out later restitution of material components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of physiological/nutritional reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how nutrition and bodily assimilation operate (chyle, separation of nutritive parts) to answer worries like cannibalism or the mixing of eaten human flesh into another's body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue from observed facts about digestion and bodily renewal (food does not permanently add indefinitely to body mass; assimilated particles are reallocated) to show that being eaten does not make re-identification impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite natural preservation to rebut corruption objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Invoke known cases where bodies or parts are preserved from corruption (cold climates, embalming, spirits of wine, sharp air) to show parts can remain intact enough for later restoration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide historical or geographical examples (Greenland preservation, high mountain preservation, embalming practices) as empirical counters to claims that decay makes resurrection impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective affinity and combination examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Use instances where particular agents selectively combine with appropriate substances (load-stone attracting iron from mixture, solvents dissolving one component) to show that proper recombination of parts is plausible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present selective-action examples from mechanics, magnetism, and chemistry to illustrate how complex mixtures can resolve into ordered assemblies without miraculous violation of natural laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argue from parity with original creation
rubrics_metrics.description: Point out that the Creator once formed bodies from earth and particles; thus re-forming them later is not more impossible than first formation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize parity: since God made bodies originally by organizing matter, the same or greater power suffices to reorganize dispersed parts into the same or suitable bodies; this theological point complements empirical analogies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use probabilistic and inductive reasoning from recurring patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Infer likelihoods from repeated observations (e.g., seasonal patterns, farmers' experiences about winds and hay harvests) to support claims about natural regularities relevant to the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ reports of recurrent natural patterns as probabilistic support—show that repeated phenomena (winds, growth patterns) yield reasonable inferences about the operation of nature that undermine objectors' claims of impossibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not require full mechanistic explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is sufficient to show experiments and effects; one need not know or defend every underlying natural hypothesis to argue possibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text advises that demonstrable facts and experiments suffice for the argument's aims; avoid getting bogged down in metaphysical theories of how particles move so long as the empirical phenomena are credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine Scripture with natural reason and divine power
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Scriptural affirmations about resurrection together with natural arguments and the acknowledgement of God's omnipotence to form a complete defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite relevant Biblical texts (e.g., Matt. xxv, Pauline passages) while insisting that understanding Scripture rightly requires appreciating the Creator's power; integrate theological and natural considerations rather than isolating them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate plausibility via many small-scale analogues
rubrics_metrics.description: Accumulate a variety of small, concrete examples (chemical, botanical, mechanical, optical, physiological) so that the aggregate force of analogies makes the central claim plausible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As the author does, marshal diverse instances across domains—embalming, optics, seed growth, magnetism, chemistry—to build a cumulative case against the charge of impossibility.
